(iv)       Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the    Ministry are still awaited:
Para Nos. 29, 75 & 78, 80, 115, 118, 128 and 137                                 Total- 7
3.         The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which have been categorized as interim
 replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the earliest.
4.         On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee  has made observations on each item of Action
 taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry.  The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Eighty-eighth  Report,
 action taken thereon by the Ministry, and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has
 been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
ASSESSMENT OF ANNUAL PLAN 2004-05 AND ALLOCATION FOR    2005-06
(Recommendation at Para 9)
5.         The Committee notes that Ministry of Civil Aviation has failed to fully utilize the outlay approved during 2004-05. 
 The Ministry anticipated to utilize an amount of Rs.1473.03 crore out of the approved allocation of Rs.1620.98 crore during
 the year 2004-05, which exemplifies the poor financial management in the Ministry of Civil Aviation.  The Committee feels
 that there is a lack of proper planning in the various organizations of Ministry of Civil Aviation, as a result of which the
 Ministry was unable to utilize optimally the approved outlays at its disposal.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
 the Ministry of Civil Aviation should impress upon the concerned agencies to make a realistic assessment of their financial
 requirements so that the allocations made do not remain unutilized.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
6.         The observations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.  Due care would be taken to ensure that Plan
 budgets are formulated on realistic basis so as to ensure that the same are properly utilized.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
7.         The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should formulate Plan budgets on realistic basis and also review the
 same at quarterly intervals to monitor the utilization of the allocations under different Budget Heads.  The Committee
 therefore recommends that the exercise undertaken during the preparation of Revised Budget Estimates should involve a
 detailed review of the progress of various projects rather than conducting the same in a routine manner.
INDIAN AIRLINES
(Recommendation at Para 22)
8.         The Committee would like to record its appreciation regarding the role played by Indian Airlines and Alliance Air in
 evacuation of people from Andaman & Nicobar Islands after the tsunami disaster and heavy snowfall in parts of Jammu &
 Kashmir in the winter season this year.    The Committee notes that Indian Airlines is expected to earn a profit of Rs.8.75
 crores by the end of the financial year 2004-05.   The Committee understands the reasons for the low amount of profit likely
 to be earned by Indian Airlines.   The Committee observes that Indian Airlines does not have sufficient number of aircraft to
 optimally utilize the domestic seat capacity available in the country and the average age of the aircraft available with Indian
 Airlines is on the higher side.   Also Indian Airlines has to take the lion's share in undertaking social responsibilities of the
 nation.   As part of its social obligation, Indian Airlines also has to fly to those unremunerative destinations, which other
 airlines choose not to fly due to commercial considerations.   The Committee, therefore, appreciates that, inspite of the odds
 being placed heavily against the company, Indian Airlines would be ending the financial year 2004-05 with marginal profits.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
9.         Ministry of Civil Aviation would like to thank the Committee for its views with regard to role and financial
 performance of Indian Airlines/Alliance Air.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
            10.       The Committee desires that Indian Airlines/Alliance Air would maintain their special role in fulfilling the
 social obligations of the nation especially during the times of extreme distress.
(Recommendation at Para 26)
11.       The Committee notes that the revision of scales of pay of employees of Indian Airlines had become due on 1.1.1997.  
 However, even after a lapse of a period of more than eight years, the Government is yet to take a decision in the matter.  
 The Committee feels that the revision of scales of pay would contribute towards preventing the exodus of trained manpower
 from Indian Airlines.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take an early decision in the
 matter so that the employees of Indian Airlines are not deprived of their legitimate right to the revision of scales of pay
 which has been pending for long.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
12.       The Government has noted the recommendation.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
13.       The Committee expresses its anguish over the evasive comments of the Ministry offered in response to the

96threport of Standing Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/96threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:22]
 recommendation of the Parliamentary Committee.  The Committee is extremely unhappy about the lackadaisical approach of
 the Ministry on the issue of revision of scales of pay of employees of Indian Airlines.  The Committee is of the view that the
 satisfaction level of the personnel in the matter of service conditions is a major factor affecting the performance of any
 organisation.  The total inaction on the part of the Ministry in the matter of pay revision of employees of Indian Airlines is
 surprising especially in the present age of poaching and stiff competition by other Indian scheduled carriers.  The
 Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Ministry should expedite its decision in the matter in the overall interest of the
 employees and the organisation. 
(Recommendation at Para 29)
 
14.       The Committee observes that the issues relating to acquisition of aircraft for Indian Airlines has been lingering on for
 a long time.   The Committee welcomes the decision of the Government to augment the fleet of Indian Airlines through
 acquisition of aircraft.   The Committee recommends that all further actions in this context should be taken on priority basis
 and the actual fleet acquisition process should begin at the earliest.   However, the Committee notes that there are some
 distributing news in the press regarding the pricing of the aircraft being procured by Indian Airlines.   The Committee
 recommends that adequate care should be taken while concluding the aircraft deal so that the acquisition of aircraft is carried
 out in the best interests of Indian Airlines and the nation.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
15.       The Government has taken note of the paras report regarding sale of A 320 aircraft by Airbus Industries to Air Asia at
 a price much lower than IAL and clarification has been obtained in the matter. Based on the further negotiations held with
 the manufacturers, it has been possible to obtain additional concessions/discounts and formal sanction of the Government for
 purchase of 43 aircraft by IAL is expected to be issued shortly. 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
16.       The Committee notes the reply and is happy to note that the Ministry has now taken due cognizance of its
 apprehensions regarding the pricing of aircrafts being procured by Indian Airlines. The Committee desires that the actual
 acquisition of aircrafts would now commence at the earliest in the best interest of Indian Airlines and the nation.
OPENING OF INTERNATIONAL ROUTES FOR PRIVATE AIRLINES
(Recommendation at Para 32)
17.       The Committee is not convinced with the reply given by the Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding its decision to open
 up international skies to a particular airlines and granting it passage rights to some international routes on the opening day of
 its public offer. The Committee is of the view that the timing of the decision pushed up the company’s IPO prospects and the
 policy adopted by the Government and the clearances granted by the Ministry to the company were too close to the public
 offer of the company to be termed as coincidence.  The Committee feels that grant of speedy clearances to the company
 helped the airline get a good opening for its equity offering.  The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the conduct of
 Ministry of Civil Aviation in granting speedy clearances to the airline and the policy changes should be further enquired into
 by an independent agency.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
18.       Minister (Civil Aviation) has clarified the position of the Government in a statement made in the Rajya Sabha on
 13.05.2005.  It is reiterated that the decision to permit Indian scheduled airlines to operate to foreign destinations was the
 culmination of a long process and was consciously taken after due consideration.
 19.      Requests for allowing private airlines to operate on international routes were received in the Ministry for the past
 several years from various quarters like industry associations and trade bodies as well as Ministries like Tourism. It was
 emphasised that this would help in better utilisation of India’s bilateral rights, improve connectivity and create business
 opportunities within the country, which in turn would help the national economy as a whole.
 
20.       In fact, the process to allow Indian scheduled carriers to fly abroad began as early as October, 2003 with the
 announcement of the Prime Minister during the visit of Sri Lankan Prime Minister to permit private airlines of India to fly to
 Sri Lanka.  In December 2003, the Government decided to also allow private airlines to operate to all SAARC countries. In
 pursuance of these decisions, two private airlines - Jet Airways and Air Sahara - commenced operations to Sri Lanka and
 Nepal. It is, therefore, pertinent to mention that the policy to allow private carriers to operate abroad is not a recent one. 
21.       The Naresh Chandra Committee, constituted to prepare a road map for the civil aviation sector in their report
 submitted in December 2003, also recommended that private airlines be allowed to operate on international routes in view of
 the under utilisation of capacity in the international segment, particularly during peak season. The Committee also noted that
 India was using barely 40% of its bilateral rights.
22.       In the Cabinet Meeting held on 10.12.2003, while allowing private airlines to operate to SAARC countries, the
 Cabinet also directed Ministry of Civil Aviation to bring up a comprehensive note on liberalising international air services. 
 In pursuance of this decision, a proposal was initiated for allowing private airlines to operate on international routes except

96threport of Standing Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/96threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:22]
 Gulf countries. This proposal was considered by the previous Government in the Cabinet Meeting held on 4.2.2004.  
 However, a decision on this proposal was postponed.
23.       After the present Government assumed office, the Cabinet in its meeting on 8 th September, 2004, while approving
 this Ministry’s proposal to sign the Air Services Agreement with Tunisia, directed the Ministry to bring up a proposal for
 building up of capacity both in public and private sector for operation of air services for optimum utilisation of our bilateral
 rights.
24.       Accordingly, a proposal to allow private airlines to operate on international sectors except the Gulf countries was
 inter alia placed before the Cabinet after following all established procedures. The draft Cabinet note was circulated to all
 concerned Ministries on 10.11.2004 and after receipt of their comments, the proposal was sent to Cabinet Secretariat in
 December 2004. Thereafter, the Cabinet considered and approved the proposal in its meeting on 29.12.2004.  Thus, it may
 be observed that the proposal was moved in accordance with Cabinet’s directions and the necessary procedures were fully
 adhered to. 
25.       It may also be mentioned that the contention that rights were allocated to a particular airline on the opening day of its
 public offer does not appear to be factually correct. In pursuance of Government’s decision taken on 29.12.2004, the first
 traffic rights were allocated to Air India and other Indian scheduled carriers for operations to UK on 31.01.2005, as the
 airlines were required to confirm their entitlements to the UK authorities for slot allocation at UK airports. However, this
 date has no relevance to the IPO offer of a private airline, as the opening day of the IPO issue of a particular airline was
 apparently on 18.02.2005. In any case, Government’s decisions were in no way guided by the dates of issue of IPO’s of
 private companies. 
26.       It is, therefore, evident that the decision to allow Indian scheduled carriers to operate on international routes was the
 culmination of a well considered process over a period of one year, starting in December 2003. The sequence of events
 clearly reveals that the Government decision had nothing to do with the IPO issue of any airline. It was entirely based on the
 need to allow Indian carriers to optimise our entitlements vis-à-vis foreign airlines. In view of the facts enumerated, no
 enquiry into this issue by an independent agency is warranted, since this Ministry has been fully transparent in its processes,
 has adhered to all procedures and no issue emerges that needs to be investigated.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
27.       The Committee notes that the reply furnished by the Ministry which consists of the details of the process of decision
 making in the matter of allowing Indian scheduled carriers/private airlines to operate on international routes except the Gulf
 countries.  However, the Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry has given evasive reply to the main issue in
 question regarding the grant of speedy clearances to a particular airline in pursuance of above decision.  The Committee
 feels that if the Ministry is confident about the legality and transparency of the matter, as it has been attempted to be made
 out in the reply, there should be no objection against an inquiry by an independent agency.  The Committee, therefore,
 reiterates its recommendation that the matter of grant of speedy clearances to the particular airlines to enhance its IPO
 prospects, after the decision of the Government to allow Indian scheduled Carriers to operate on international routes, should
 be inquired into by an independent agency. 
(Recommendation at Para 35)
28.       The Committee is not convinced with the reply furnished by Ministry of Civil Aviation with regard to the criteria
 adopted in selection of scheduled domestic airlines to be allowed to fly on international routes.  The Committee feels that
 there is an element of arbitrariness in imposing restrictions on airlines in terms of experience of flying etc. and not allowing
 all the domestic scheduled airlines to fly on international routes.  By imposing such restrictions, the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation did not give a fair chance to the other scheduled domestic private airline operating in the country.  The Committee
 is also of the view that Ministry of Civil Aviation did not carry out any due diligence of the performance record of the
 existing private sector airlines in terms of fulfilling the social obligations by flying to remote and inaccessible areas of the
 country and utilizing the costly technologies installed at the airports such a ILS CAT-III system.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
29.       Minister (Civil Aviation) has clarified the position of the Government in a statement made in the Rajya Sabha on
 13.05.2005.  The minimum requirement prescribed for airlines to qualify for operations on international routes is entirely
 based on the consideration that only airlines with proven track records in the domestic sectors should be allowed to operate
 internationally. This is particularly important, as the Government does not want airlines to withdraw or curtail operations on
 domestic routes once they start international operations. Therefore, a minimum fleet strength of 20 aircraft has been
 prescribed. This would ensure sustained domestic connectivity while enabling the airlines to gain greater experience and put
 in place the required infrastructure facilities for operation on international routes at a later stage. 
30.       The eligibility criteria of five years’ operation in the domestic sector is also a carefully thought-out decision based on
 advice received from the safety regulator, Director General of Civil Aviation (DGCA). Experience of five years’ operations
 in domestic sector was considered necessary as a start up airline invariably needs that much time to put its entire
 maintenance and other safety related systems in place. It may be appreciated that once airlines start operating to foreign
 countries, they would be subject to safety checks by regulatory authorities of other countries. It is, therefore, essential that

96threport of Standing Committee On Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/96threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:22]
 airlines first stabilise operations in the domestic sectors and establish the requisite safety/maintenance standards before they
 are considered for international operations.
31.       It may also be mentioned that on the date of Government decision in this regard, i.e. 29.12.2004, there were only
 three private scheduled airlines operating on domestic sectors.  Out of the three, two qualified for international operations as
 per the eligibility criteria decided. One airline, which did not qualify, was in any case only about one year old and had also
 not shown any interest in international operations. Therefore, there was no discrimination against any airline as such. 
32.       As regards due diligence and performance records of airlines, once an airline has operated in domestic sectors for 5
 years in accordance with the laid down standards, its track record in safety and overall performance would have been
 adequately monitored by DGCA. There are stringent safety requirements that the airlines are required to follow while
 operating on domestic sector and each of the airlines is also required to meet social obligations by adhering to route
 dispersal guidelines.  There is strict monitoring of their adherence to the route dispersal guidelines on a monthly basis by the
 DGCA.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
33.       The Committee notes from the reply of the Ministry that there are only two minimum eligibility criteria prescribed
 for selection of scheduled domestic airlines to be allowed to operate on international routes, namely, a minimum fleet
 strength of 20 aircrafts and a minimum experience of five years operations on domestic routes.  The Committee also notes
 that the basic policy of the Government to allow the scheduled carriers to operate on international routes has been framed
 after due consideration of the Report of Naresh Chandra Committee, which was submitted to the Ministry in December
 2003.  The said committee had reportedly revealed that we are presently using only 40% of our bilateral rights.  However,
 the Committee feels that the steep restrictions imposed by the Ministry are impediments in achieving the basic objectives
 behind the new policy to mitigate under capacity in the international segment and to enhance global connectivity to and
 from different states in the country.   The Committee recommends that in view of the irreversible nature of the new policy,
 the Ministry should review its prescribed standards regarding fleet strength, maintenance facilities, safety systems etc. for
 granting licences to new airlines in the domestic sector, taking into consideration the requirements for the international
 sector also.  Such a review would enable the relaxation of the existing stringent restrictions on Indian scheduled airlines for
 international operations. The Committee also notes that the stringent restrictions have not been able to avoid the denial of
 flights to one of the private airlines to destinations in the United States of America.
(Recommendation at Para 39)
34.       The Committee notes that there is a contradiction between the objectives stated by the Ministry of Civil Aviation in
 allowing private airlines to fly to international destinations and the routes actually allotted by the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 to the private airlines.  The Committee observes that the basic objective of the Government in allowing private airlines to fly
 to international destinations was providing connectivity to such destination which the Ministry has not been able to provide
 in the past because of lack of capacity of Air India and Indian Airlines.  However, the Ministry of Civil Aviation has granted
 permission to these private airlines to fly to those destinations, which were already being serviced, by Air India and Indian
 Airlines.  Hence the stated position of the Government in this respect is in total contradiction with the actual decisions of the
 Government and the basic objective of the Government to provide connectivity to new international destinations has been
 defeated.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
35.       While it is the intention of the Ministry to encourage operation of eligible airlines to newer destinations, it may be
 emphasised that the primary objective behind the decision to permit Indian scheduled carriers to fly abroad is to ensure
 optimal utilisation of traffic rights available to India. The traffic rights available to India through various bilateral
 agreements were under-utilised for a variety of reasons.
36.       India offers tremendous opportunities to airlines because of the rapidly growing international traffic to/from this
 country.  This potential was largely exploited by foreign airlines. While it is true that most of the routes so far allocated to
 Indian scheduled airlines are also being served by Air India/Indian Airlines, this would ensure better utilisation of the traffic
 rights available with us. Otherwise, the traffic on these routes would have been diverted to foreign airlines allowing them to
 derive disproportionate benefits.  It would not be desirable if foreign airlines  were allowed to carry traffic to/from India in
 increasing numbers while restricting our own airlines – public or private – from operating on international routes. 
37.       It may also be mentioned that most of the routes allocated to foreign airlines have witnessed significant growth of
 traffic in recent past and therefore provide ample commercial opportunities to all airlines.  It is also the considered view of
 the Ministry that direct connectivity between point-to-point destinations needs to be encouraged.  For instance, if the traffic
 size between UK and India is significant, the commercial opportunities out of this demand should ideally be utilised by
 Indian carriers or carriers of UK. The Government have approached the issue of liberalization of international air services
 with these objectives in mind. 
38.       It may also be emphasised that implementation of the policy is still at an early stage. As the process evolves,
 Government will continue to take stock of the situation and it is inevitable that newer destinations will get added over a
 period of time.

file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/96threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:09:22]
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
39.       The Committee is not satisfied with the reply.  The Ministry has not charted out any long-term plan for the
 implementation of the new policy of opening up the international skies to the Indian scheduled airlines.  The Committee
 recommends that the Ministry should frame a comprehensive plan identifying international sectors to be covered by Air
 India/Indian Airlines/International Scheduled Carriers so as to avoid any conflict of interests and at the same time ensuring
 full realization of the objective to enhance utilization of traffic rights available to India.  
 
REVIEW OF ROUTE DISPERSAL GUIDELINES
(Recommendation at Para 42)
 40.      The Committee is of the view that the present aviation policy being followed by the Government has not been
 effective in making the private airlines share the social obligations of the country.  The Committee feels that the private
 airlines have been focusing on lucrative trunk routes only.  These airlines have been operating only on the basis of
 commercial terms and tend to follow the bare minimum of what is mandatory for them under the Route Dispersal
 Guidelines. The Committee recommends that the Route Dispersal Guidelines should be revisited to ensure that the private
 domestic airlines also share the social obligation of connecting remote parts of the country in the true sense and not by
 merely completing the formalities in this regard.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
41.       The Route Dispersal Guidelines (RDG) issued by the Government in 1994, require all scheduled airlines to deploy at
 least 10% of the capacity deployed by them on major trunk routes (i.e. CAT-I routes) on the routes to/from North East,
 Jammu & Kashmir, Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands (i.e. CAT II routes). Out of the total capacity so
 deployed in CAT-II routes, 10 % of the capacity is required to be deployed for connectivity with North East, Jammu &
 Kashmir, Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Further, the airlines are also required to deploy 50% of the
 capacity, deployed on CAT-I routes, on non-trunk routes i.e. CAT-III routes. The Director General of Civil Aviation
 monitors the compliance with the RDG on a monthly basis.
42.       The Government had set-up a Committee under the Chairmanship of Director General of Civil Aviation vide Order
 dated 23.9.2003 to review the existing Route Dispersal Guidelines. The Committee has   submitted its report on 18.3.2005,
 which is under active consideration of the Government. The concerns expressed by the Committee shall be duly considered
 before taking any final decision in the matter. The private airlines are also being apprised about these concerns for
 appropriate action.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
43.       The Committee fails to understand the nature and reasons for the inordinate delay by DGCA and that of the Ministry,
 of over nine months to come out with a specific time frame for accepting the recommendation. The Committee recommends
 that the matter be expedited with desired pace.
REQUIREMENT OF TRAINED MANPOWER
(Recommendation at Para 50)
 
44.       The Committee is of the view that as per the policy being pursued by the Government in granting licenses to new

HIGH COST OF AIR TURBINE FUEL (ATF)
(Recommendations at Paras 75 and 78)
63.       Fuel plays a crucial role in the cost structure and profitability of any airline. High cost of ATF in the country
 increases the cost of operation. The Committee welcomes the proposed amendment in the Central Sales Tax Act whereby
 sales tax on bonded ATF uplifted for international operation would be exempted. The Committee is hopeful that this move
 would, to some extent, help our national carriers strengthen their financial position.  The Committee, however, is concerned
 to note that some states which had earlier taken initiative and reduced sales tax on ATF, have retracted and imposed high
 rates of sales tax on ATF.,  The Committee recommends that Ministry of Finance should consider and give approval  to the
 proposal of Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding notifying ATF as ‘Declared Good’ under Section 14 of Central Sales Tax
 Act on priority basis so that sales tax on ATF could be contained with the maximum rate of 4%. The Committee further
 recommends that the Ministry of Finance may also discuss the issue with the State Governments and try to convince them
 that the reduction in the sales tax on ATF will certainly increase the efficiency and viability of our carriers.
64.       The Committee recommends that the Government should create conditions, which provide wider choice to the airline
 companies for procurement of ATF. The Committee hopes that this step would promote competition among the suppliers
 and help lowering the rates of ATF to some extent.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
65.       ATF is a major cost component of airlines in India. It constitutes about 35% of total operating cost for domestic
 operations.
 
66.       Two reasons for high price of ATF in India are:
 
(i)   High rate of sales tax charged by State Governments on ATF sold to domestic flights.
(ii)  High marketing and distribution margins charged by Oil PSUs, which are in monopoly situation for supply of ATF.
67.       As per notification issued under section 5 of Central Sales Tax Act (CST) w.e.f. 7
th June, 2005, there would be no
 sales tax on ATF purchased for international flights of designated Indian Carrier. This would bring Indian designated carries
 at par with foreign carriers, which are already getting sales tax exemption on ATF purchase.
68.       With a view to reduce the incidence of sales tax, it has been suggested to the Finance Ministry that ATF sold to
 domestic flights may be notified as ‘Declared Goods’ under Section 14  of the Central Sales Tax Act, so as to cap the rate of
 Sales Tax on ATF to 4%. Finance Ministry has, however, informed that the proposal could not be agreed to due to serious
 revenue implications for the State Governments.  ATF sold to turbo-prop aircraft is already notified as ‘Declared Goods’
 under Section 14 of the Central Sales Tax Act attracting 4% sales tax on ATF.
69.       The State Governments may get affected only marginally by the above measure. But, these would go a long way in
 improving the health of the aviation industry in the country and ultimately fostering the economy, tourism and regional
 development to a great extent.

 (Recommendations at Para 86)
71.       The Committee is of the view that, as brought out by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, the proposals of Fringe Benefits
 Tax, if implemented on the airlines industry, would have a major financial impact on airlines operators.   The Committee is
 of the view that the elements brought out in para 84 above do not truly form part of benefits being given to the employees.  
 In fact, these are clear-cut major cost components for the functioning of airlines and should not be considered as qualifying
 factors for the imposition of Fringe Benefit Tax as proposed in the Budget.   Imposition of tax on the above stated cost
 elements would adversely affect the profitability of the airlines, which have very recently started coming out of the
 recessionary trend.   Further, the imposition of tax on aircraft repair, running and maintenance expenses (including
 depreciation) and consumption of fuel will directly raise the cost of operations.   This may result in fare increase, thereby
 making the air travel costlier.   Further, treating the main operating costs of airlines at par with fringe benefits appears to be
 illogical.    Taxing such cost is not in consonance with the basic objective of this new levy.   The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that Ministry of Finance should reconsider its decision and recognizing the peculiarity of the nature of working
 of the airlines industry, exclude the expenditure on items mentioned in para 84 above from the purview of the Fringe
 Benefits Tax.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
72.       Ministry of Finance has duly considered Airline’s plea in respect of expenditure incurred on repairs running and
 maintenance of aircraft, consumption of fuel and depreciation on aircraft. Recognizing that these are major cost components
 for functioning of airlines and in no way result in any fringe benefit to employees, these items have been removed from the
 ambit of fringe benefit tax when the bill was finally passed.
73.       The cost of free or concessional ticket for private journeys of employees or their family members and expenditure
 incurred by airlines on Crew Hotel accommodation and foreign travel expenses has not been removed from the purview of
 FBT. The free and concessional tickets provided to employees is on a ‘subject to load’ basis and are made available to the
 employees in accordance with the IATA Resolutions. As per the provisions of FBT, the valuation of these tickets has to be
 made at a value at which these tickets are offered to the public. It is very relevant that such tickets cannot be offered to the
 public and hence such tickets have no market value. Therefore, the value of such free concessional tickets is not
 determinable. It may be pertinent to mention that the airline employees are provided seats on a subject to availability basis
 and that to at the last moment that is prior to departure of the flight.  Where the business of the enterprise itself is carriage of
 passengers and where such enterprise does not provide any LTC facility to its employees, such free concessional tickets
 should be outside the purview of FBT.
74.       In the course of conduct of the business, the crew is required to travel in the aircraft and stay in hotel which is a
 necessity in course of their flight duties and it cannot be stated that benefit accrues to the crew out of such travel and stay at
 hotel. Considering the peculiar nature of the airline business, crew hotel expenses and foreign travel expenses in case of
 airlines needs to be excluded from the purview of FBT.
75.       The matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance.

82.       The Government had decided to restructure in the year 2000 the four metro airports of Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and
 Kolkata through leasing route.  However, the legal process for introducing a suitable amendment in the AAI Act, 1994 could

 officers constituted for this purpose under the chairmanship of Member (Finance), AAI.  It was found that the concept of

 developed into a comprehensive alternate plan.  Since October, 2004, a number of meetings have been held between

92.       The Committee is not convinced with the replies furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation with regard to the
 modernisation and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports.  The Committee is of the opinion that modernisation is not
 merely about the provision of facilities and expansion of the terminal buildings of the airports. It should also increase the
 capacity of the airports to handle more flights, by construction of additional runways, which does not seem to be a
 probability in case of Mumbai airport. The Committee further notes that a major chunk of the profit from airports in
 generated from Mumbai and Delhi airports and it is these two airports that the Government proposes to restructure and
 modernize through the joint venture route. The Committee understands that the revenue generated by the Government from
 the profit making airports is used to fulfill the developmental needs as well as day-to-day activities of the other airports.  The
 Committee fails to understand as to how the Government would fulfill the developmental needs of the other airports after the
 management of these airports is passed on to the Joint Venture Companies.  The sustained existence of such airports would
 become difficult in such a scenario.  The Committee is in favour of modernisation of the Mumbai and Delhi airports, but not
 at the cost of the other airports in the country maintained by the Airports Authority of India. The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the Government should re-look at the modernisation process of Delhi and Mumbai airports so that the
 development and maintenance of the other airports in the country is not compromised.

 of reassessing its strategy, the Ministry is following the unhealthy policy of creation of monopoly by promoting only one
 airport at different metros, as in the case of Delhi and Mumbai. The Committee also notes that the justification put forward
 by the Ministry for the closure of the existing airport at Hyderabad is contrary to the rationale of the Ministry for rejecting
 the proposals for Greenfield airports at Delhi and Mumbai.  In respect of those two airports, the Ministry has maintained
 throughout that unless the capacity is not optimized or added in the existing Brownfield airport, it is not prudent to set up a
 Greenfield airport.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Government should reconsider the decision to close down
 the existing airport at Hyderabad on the commissioning of a new International airport.(Para 104)
PROTECTION TO THE INTERESTS OF THE EMPLOYEES OF AIRPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA.
 
            The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and finds that there is no assurance of protection of the existing terms
 and condition of service of the employees of Airports Authority of India after restructuring of Delhi/Mumbai airports.  With
 respect to Greenfield airports of Bangalore and Hyderabad, the Committee is not satisfied with the reply that Government

 fair basis. (Para 108)
CREATION OF A EASTERN HUB AT KOLKATA
            The Committee notes the reply and finds that the Ministry has not mentioned anything about the recommendation for
 the creation of a southern hub at Chennai.  Further, the reply has not indicated the details of the work undertaken at Chennai
 airport.  The Committee desires that air hubs at Kolkata and Chennai will be created very soon and airlines would be given
 incentives for use of these airports for parking etc. by levying lesser charges.(Para 119)
 
PAWAN HANS HELICOPTERS LIMITED
 
            The Committee notes the reply and feels that the Ministry has not fully appreciated its recommendation.  There is no
 denying the fact that helicopter services could not be a viable alternate mode of travel in those places where fixed wing
 aircrafts are operating presently.  The Committee is of the view that if the Ministry finds the non-accessible tourist
 destinations non-viable for operations by PHHL, it should at least offer attractive terms and conditions for the wet lease of
 helicopters to State Governments/Government agencies/Private parties to enable them to tap the tourism potential in various
 parts of the country. (Para 130)
 
            The Committee is not satisfied with the reply furnished by the Ministry.  The Committee has not been apprised about
 the details of the safety audits of the Helicopter operators and instead a routine reply that ‘safety audits are being conducted
 on continuous basis’ has been given.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry should evolve permanent mechanism
 viz. constitution of a Helicopter Cell, to monitor the helicopter operations in view of the Kaushik Committee Report.  As
 regards the proficiency rating system of pilots in DGCA, the Ministry vide  O.M. No.A.60011/020/2005-VE dated 4
th May,
 2005 had informed, inter-alia, that the lone post of Flight Inspector (Helicopter) in the Office of DGCA fell vacant in
 December 2001 and the same was filled up on ad-hoc basis for one year w.e.f. 16
th August 2003.  This post has again fallen
 vacant as the appointee was unwilling to continue beyond one year and was relieved of his duties w.e.f. 16 th August 2004. 
 Accordingly, this post was re-advertised.  The Ministry has, however, not informed whether the same has been filled up
 now.  The Ministry further informed that proficiency checks of Pilots are conducted by Examiners approved by DGCA, on
 bi-annual basis to comply with the requirements of the Aircraft Rules, 1937.  The Committee notes that the DGCA Inspector
 is associated as an observer in those cases where consecutive checks are carried out by the same examiner to ensure sanctity
 of the proficiency check.    The Committee finds that the reply is highly insufficient on the procedure for proficiency checks
 of the pilots.  The Committee is surprised to note that the post of Flight Inspector (Helicopter) has been lying vacant for long

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the
 Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this Ninety-seventh Report of the Committee on Action Taken by the Government on the
 Recommendations/Observations of the Committee contained in its Ninetieth Report on the ‘Development of Airport Sector with special emphasis on

2.    The Ninetieth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented to the
 Parliament on the  23
rd August 2005. 
3.    The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its Ninetieth Report were received from the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation on 18th November 2005.
4.    The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 22nd February 2006.
 
NEW DELHI ;
February 
22, 2006
Phalguna 3, 1927 (Saka)                                             
                          NILOTPAL BASU     
    Chairman
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
 Tourism & Culture.
 
R E P O R T
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the observations/ recommendations as
 contained in its Ninetieth Report on  “Development of Airport Sector with Special Emphasis on new Modern Airports”, which was presented to both
 the Houses of Parliament on 23rd August, 2005.
 2.         Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 18 th November, 2005 in respect of all the
 observations/recommendations contained in the Report, which have been categorised as follows: -
(i)         Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry:
              Para Nos.: 51, 65                                                                                                    Total- 2
(ii)        Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Ministry’s replies:
Para Nos.:  Nil                                                                                                       Total- Nil
(iii)       Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not been accepted by the Committee:
Para Nos.: 43, 49, 54, 56, 61                                                                                    Total- 5
(iv)       Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry are still awaited:
Para Nos.:  20, 21, 26, 31, 46, 62, 70, 82, 86, 90                                                    Total- 10
3.         The Committee desires that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee
 should be furnished to it at the earliest.
4.         On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the
 Ministry.  The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Ninetieth Report, action taken thereon by the Ministry, and
 recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
 
MODERNISATION AND RESTRUCTURING OF DELHI AND MUMBAI AIRPORTS
(Recommendation at Para 20)
 
5.         The Committee is constrained to note that the proposal regarding modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports has been
 lingering on for a fairly long period and still the Government has not been able to come up with any concrete plans in this regard.  The Ministry of
 Civil Aviation has also not been able to even firm up the financial requirements for these projects.  The Government has been quoting different cost
 estimates at different stage.  The Committee also notes that the initial figures of Rs.10, 000 crore to Rs.20, 000 crore stated by the Secretary of the
 Ministry were too inflated and also gave the impression that the money was required immediately in one go which in fact was actually required in
 phases spread over 15 to 20 years.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
6.         Union Cabinet took decision in the year 2000 to restructure Delhi and Mumbai airports through long term lease.  However, while the process
 went along, it was found that AAI Act needed amendment to enable the process to move through long term lease route. The Government took steps
 to amend the AAI Act 1994.  It took nearly three and half Years to carry the amendment.  Finally the amendment was approved by the Parliament in
 July 2003.  The Union Cabinet in Sept 2003 decided to restructure Delhi and Mumbai airports through JV route involving leasing of assets. 
 Accordingly an Empowered Group of Ministers was appointed.  After undertaking extensive due diligence at various levels now the modernization
 and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports is at the final stage.  The technical and financial bids have been received on 14.9.2005 and are at
 evaluation stage. The Government has a well determined mode and plan of the process of modernization of these airports.
 
7.         The delay in this process has been mainly on account of legal problems, in-depth and intense Inter-ministerial consultations as this transaction
 was first of its kind both in terms of scope and complexity.  The airports are to be developed by the Joint Venture Company (JVC) which will
 necessarily have a world class airport operator. Apart from executing the mandated capital expenditure within 2 and 5 years of the effective date, the
 JVC will have to adhere to the initial development plan submitted at the time of bidding and the Master Plan to be submitted to the Govt. within six
 months of the signing of the agreement.

8.         The variance in cost estimates occurred because they have been furnished at different points of time when the Global Technical Adviser was
 still working on its report. Capital expenditure is to be carried out over a period of 20 years broken into 4 stages of 5 year each and linked with the
 traffic trigger with substantial capital expenditure envisaged in Phase I i.e. 2005 to 2009. The estimates do not include the expenditure to be incurred
 by AAI for modernizing the ATC etc.  It also does not include expenditure which could be incurred by other public agencies for instance, Delhi
 Metro, NHAI, Delhi Water Supply, BSES, etc.  Further, nothing prevents JVC to incur more expenditure if it is warranted by the expected traffic.
 More traffic would mean more revenue and therefore there would be incentive for JVC to enhance capacity to get more traffic. If traffic trigger
 requires early and heavier investment, the JVC is incentivised to undertake the investment accordingly. In the light of the above even the initial
 figures of Rs.10000 to Rs.20000 crore for both the airports may not be unrealistic. This figure is less than the investment incurred at other
 international airports with world class standards. It has been estimated that the capital investment to the extent of Rs.7961 crores and Rs.6131 crores
 will be required for Delhi and Mumbai airports, respectively over a period of 20 years in phases.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
9.         The Committee is not convinced with the reply put forth by the Ministry and observes that clear-cut statistics with regard to modernization of
 airports should be given to the public and the Parliament.  As the proposal regarding modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai Airports
 involves huge expenditure and also determines the future of aviation sector in this country, the exaggerated initial cost estimates indicate poor
 financial planning.  The Committee feels that the unrealistic cost estimates at the planning stage might have swayed the decision in favour of the
 Joint Venture route. 
 (Recommendation at Para 21)
10.       The Committee feels that the process of modernization as explained by the Ministry, is very slow and the target to be achieved is also minimal
 in terms of global standards.  The Committee observes that Airport Authority of India at present has already achieved the target with the present rate
 of investment.  The Committee does not agree with the Ministry of Civil Aviation that resource crunch is the main reason for inviting private sector
 participation for the modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai Airports.  The quantum of investment which is to the tune of Rs.13, 786
 crore, required for modernization of Delhi and Mumbai airports is not on the higher side and that too is required in a manner over a period of 15 to
 20 years.  The Committee feels that the Government can even mobilize the funds required.  This will ensure not only the management control of the
 proposed operators of the airports in the hands of Indian nationals but also result in protecting the safety, security and sovereignty of the country.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 11.      The decision to restructure and modernize airports through PPP route is a widely prevalent public policy tool and is not primarily dictated by
 the resource crunch faced by the Government. The intention is to have world class airport and world class management with the world class airport
 operator under public private partnership. While Government can mobilize the funds such funds are more needed to be used for supporting social
 sector development programmes such as health, education, social welfare, etc. In the airport sector if private investment can come it would be
 endeavour of the Government to facilitate that as the public investment saved here could be used elsewhere where it is more required such as North
 East etc.
 
12.       The airports at Delhi and Mumbai shall be managed by the JVC which will be registered in India under the Companies Act and therefore will
 function under the Indian Companies Act.  This JVC shall have the right to operate and manage the airports as per the transaction agreements singed
 within the ambit of laws of India, e.g., Indian Contract Act, Indian Arbitration Act and other applicable laws. The safety shall continue to be the
 responsibility of DGCA and there is no dilution in its authority. Security shall be the responsibility of State and there is no dilution in its
 responsibility as far as airport operated by JVC is concerned.
 
13.       In the JVC maximum FDI, which is permitted, is only 49%.  Thus, the management control of these airports remain in the hands of Indian
 nationals.  However the management of these airports is sought to be improved by involving world class airport operators in the JVC. Given the
 above the development of metro airports through the JVC route does not, in any way, compromise on safety, security and sovereignty of the country.
 In fact, the ownership of assets remain with the AAI / Govt.
 
14.       As regards performance standards, Government is aiming to achieve average global standard of 3.75
 with the aim of ultimately attaining
 standard of 4 (The highest standard of world being 4.45).  The current standards at these airports are much below the world standards. Earlier, AAI
 did not undertake survey of these airports through IATA.  This has been commissioned from January 2005 on quarterly basis.  As per the latest
 survey from April – June 2005, the average at Delhi and Mumbai airports is 2.94 and 3.06 respectively.  In case of Mumbai, the average has declined
 from 3.20 to 3.06 as recorded from Jan – March 2005 whereas at Delhi, there is a slight improvement.  It may be mentioned that survey of one or two
 quarter is not enough to judge the attainment of standards and linking with investments. In fact, the standards coveredunder IATA survey are directly
 related with the management of facilities. In this respect, AAI’s management leaves much to be desired.  AAI does not have an institutional
 mechanism to take appropriate action / curing of deficiency pointed out in the survey as there is no penalty / liquidated damage imposed on AAI for
 non-attainment of standards as against the JVC which will have penalties for the non-attainment of the same. This could even lead to termination of
 the agreement.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
15.       The Committee is not satisfied with the reply furnished by the Ministry.  The Committee is not convinced that the Government cannot
 mobilise the funds for executing the modernisation plan of Delhi and Mumbai airports on its own as the estimated quantum of investment is required
 over a period of 15 to 20 years.   Moreover, the modernisation plan for the Mumbai airport cannot address the situation beyond the year 2014. The
 Committee therefore recommends that the Government should reconsider its plans to privatise Delhi and Mumbai airports under the garb of
 modernisation and instead give a serious consideration to the workable alternate plan suggested by Airports Authority of India Employees Joint
 Forum. The Committee also recommends that the Government should immediately initiate the groundwork for Greenfield Airports in Delhi and
 Mumbai with public-private participation.  
 
16.       As regards performance standards, the Committee is sad to note that even today the Airports Authority of India does not have an institutional
 mechanism to take appropriate action / curing of deficiency, as pointed out in the survey conducted by IATA regarding performance standards, and

97thReport of Committeeon Transport, Tourism & Culture
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/97threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:10:23]
 there is no penalty / liquidated damage imposed on AAI for non-attainment of standards.  It indicates that due to lack of provision of imposing
 penalty/liquidated damage on Airports Authority of India for non-attainment of standards, AAI could not fulfill consumer satisfaction and meet
 international norms and standards. The Committee feels that this needs to be corrected.  In an era of globalisation, a major profit making PSU like the
 Airports Authority of India cannot function in an isolated manner in the aviation sector.  There should not be any compromise in terms of consumer
 satisfaction and overall compliance to international norms and standards.  Both Airports Authority of India and any other private sector entrant
 through JV route should be treated at par.  The Committee fails to understand that if Airports Authority of India lacks adequate mechanism to cure
 deficiencies and is not conforming to international performance standards, then how it is handling all other airports in the country.
 
(Recommendation at Para 26)
 
17.       The Committee notes that the Government intends to attract investment worth Rs.5825 crore spread over a period of 15 years for the
 modernization and restructuring of Mumbai airport.    The Committee has been informed by the Ministry that there is no scope of having a second
 runway at Mumbai airport which could be helpful in terms of air operations.  Further, the passenger traffic movement is also expected to go up from
 14 million in 2004 to 52 million in 2024.  The Committee also understands that by 2012, Mumbai airport would get absolute chocked.  However, the
 development plans of Ministry of Civil Aviation for Mumbai Airports goes beyond 2012 i.e. upto 2019.  The Committee fails to understand as to
 how the huge investment to be made at the airport could be justified when the existing capacity constrains would not permit capacity addition.  The
 Committee is of the opinion that modernization is not merely about the creation of facilities, expansion of the terminal buildings and putting up fancy
 malls at the airports.  It should rather increase the capacity of the airports to handle more flights, by construction of additional runways, which is
 certainly not a probability in the case of Mumbai airport.  The Committee feels that if international flights have to move around on the skies for half-
an-hour to forty-five minutes after having reached the destination, then there could be no commensurate return as far as the investment, increase in
 the number of aircraft and the number of passengers actually traveling to the airport are concerned.  The Committee is of the firm view that investing
 huge money on modernization of Mumbai airport would be waste.  The Committee is of the opinion that there are certain inherent technological
 constrains while reconstructing an existing structure, particularly in the case of Mumbai airport and the option of going in for a new Greenfield
 airport rather than proposed modernization of Mumbai airport will be more prudent.  However, some investment towards augmenting the capacity
 will have to be made to address the immediate exigencies of the situation at least till such time a new Greenfield airport comes into operation.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should rather go in for construction of a new Greenfield airport with much more capacity at
 Mumbai which would require much less investment and the efforts in this direction should begin at the earliest.  In such case both the Greenfield and
 the existing airport can compete with each other.  The Committee is also of the opinion that given the growth of aviation sector in country, the
 existing infrastructure at Delhi airport also possesses that inherent lacuna and is therefore, inadequate to handle the growth being projected for the
 future by the Government.  The Committee recommends that the Government should explore the possibility of having a Greenfield airport in Delhi
 also.
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
18.      Global Technical Adviser (GTA)’s report on airfield capacity of Mumbai states as follows:
 
(i)
                  With enhanced taxiways and enhanced ATC procedures, the existing runway could accommodate projected traffic to between 2009
 and 2014.
(ii)                With some increase in average aircraft size, the existing runway, with enhanced taxiway and ATC procedures could accommodate
 projected traffic to beyond 2014.
(iii)               A close spaced parallel runway could accommodate projected traffic levels to about 2019.
(iv)              To achieve the 20 year forecast traffic a wide spaced parallel runway would be required.
(v)                Achievement of high capacity figures is dependent on several factors, including some controlled by others (e.g. ATC, airlines). This
 will occur through gradual development over future years.
 
19.       Setting up of a runway at (iii) above requires relocation of hangars of AI, additional land and removal of obstacles in the approach pathways,
 where heavy public investment will be needed besides practical difficulties. Action at (iv) is also not practical. Action at (ii) above will add capacity
 by 50% and last to meet demand upto 2014 and beyond. Thus, the existing airport will have to cater to the traffic upto 2014. Capacity on the airside
 and terminal will need to be created to cater to the traffic upto 2014 and beyond.  The capacity on the airside will be added by taxiways, ATC
 procedures and terminal expansions, etc.  These facilities will remain at the existing airport.  Hence the investment made on these capacity will not
 be a waste but will be used by the existing airport for future.
 
20.       As regards a Greenfield airport at Mumbai, there is a proposal at planning stage for setting up a second airport linked with the above traffic
 trigger and other constraints.  As regard Delhi, the present airport can be developed to meet traffic requirement upto 80 million passengers. Hence, it
 is felt that there is no need for second Greenfield airport in Delhi immediately. There is a huge difference between the cost of incremental capacity at
 a Brownfield Airport and the cost of creating the same capacity through the Greenfield Airport. As long as the capacity is not optimized at the
 Brownfield airport, foregoing the option of creation of additional capacity at the Brownfield Airport and setting up a Greenfield Airport will not be
 prudent.

MODERNISATION AND RESTRUCTURING OF DELHI AND MUMBAI AIRPORTS
 
            The Committee is not convinced with the reply put forth by the Ministry and observes that clear-cut statistics with regard to modernization of
 airports should be given to the public and the Parliament.  As the proposal regarding modernization and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai Airports
 involves huge expenditure and also determines the future of aviation sector in this country, the exaggerated initial cost estimates indicate poor
 financial planning.  The Committee feels that the unrealistic cost estimates at the planning stage might have swayed the decision in favour of the
 Joint Venture route.   (Para 9)
 
            The Committee is not satisfied with the reply furnished by the Ministry.  The Committee is not convinced that the Government cannot
 mobilise the funds for executing the modernisation plan of Delhi and Mumbai airports on its own as the estimated quantum of investment is required
 over a period of 15 to 20 years.   Moreover, the modernisation plan for the Mumbai airport cannot address the situation beyond the year 2014. The
 Committee therefore recommends that the Government should reconsider its plans to privatise Delhi and Mumbai airports under the garb of
 modernisation and instead give a serious consideration to the workable alternate plan suggested by Airports Authority of India Employees Joint
 Forum. The Committee also recommends that the Government should immediately initiate the groundwork for Greenfield Airports in Delhi and
 Mumbai with public-private participation.   (Para 15)
 
            As regards performance standards, the Committee is sad to note that even today the Airports Authority of India does not have an institutional
 mechanism to take appropriate action / curing of deficiency, as pointed out in the survey conducted by IATA regarding performance standards, and
 there is no penalty / liquidated damage imposed on AAI for non-attainment of standards.  It indicates that due to lack of provision of imposing
 penalty/liquidated damage on Airports Authority of India for non-attainment of standards, AAI could not fulfill consumer satisfaction and meet
 international norms and standards. The Committee feels that this needs to be corrected.  In an era of globalisation, a major profit making PSU like the
 Airports Authority of India cannot function in an isolated manner in the aviation sector.  There should not be any compromise in terms of consumer
 satisfaction and overall compliance to international norms and standards.  Both Airports Authority of India and any other private sector entrant
 through JV route should be treated at par.  The Committee fails to understand that if Airports Authority of India lacks adequate mechanism to cure
 deficiencies and is not conforming to international performance standards, then how it is handling all other airports in the country. (Para 16)
 
            The Committee notes that in the assessment report of the Global Technical Advisor (GTA) on airfield capacity of Mumbai airport, it has been
 stated that with enhanced taxiways and enhanced ATC procedures, the existing runway could accommodate projected traffic to between 2009 and
 2014.  Moreover, with some increase in average aircraft size, the existing runway, with enhanced taxiway and ATC procedures could accommodate
 projected traffic to beyond 2014 and to achieve the 20 year forecast traffic, a wide spaced parallel runway would be required.  In brief, the Ministry
 is of the opinion that the existing airport will cater to traffic upto 2014 and that capacity on the airside and terminal will need to be created to cater to
 traffic upto 2014 and beyond.  (Para 23)
 
            The Committee observes that there is a contradiction in the stand of the Ministry as they first agreed that there was no scope for any further
 development on the airside at Mumbai airport since there was no scope of having a second runway at that airport which could be helpful in terms of
 air-operations.  The position now informed by the Ministry is that "There is a huge difference between the cost of incremental capacity at a
 Brownfield Airport and the cost of creating the same capacity through the Greenfield Airport. As long as the capacity is not optimized at the
 Brownfield airport, foregoing the option of creation of additional capacity at the Brownfield Airport and setting up a Greenfield Airport will not be
 prudent".(Para 24)
 
           The Committee feels that the Ministry is keeping the Committee half informed as they are now saying that "parallel or two runways not
 necessarily generate adequate capacity if well designed taxi ways and parking bays do not co-exist".   The Committee has not been informed about
 the present scheme of things and the proposed modernization programme to be undertaken in the immediate future at Mumbai/Delhi airports by the
 private sector and how much capacity is estimated to be added and whether there will be newly designed taxi ways and parking bays.     (Para 25)
 
           The Committee desires that the Ministry should atleast now apprise it clearly about (a) the traffic and cargo expected to increase in future in
 the normal course on five yearly basis; the capacity addition with modifications in the existing Brownfield airports in Mumbai and Delhi through
 modernization under JV route; (b) the expected increase in traffic/cargo after modernization of Mumbai and Delhi airports; (c) the cost estimation of
 Greenfield airports at Mumbai/Delhi and the capacity of those airports in terms of time period vis-à-vis traffic and cargo to be handled; and (d) the
 difference in the cost of modernization of the existing Brownfield airports and construction of new Greenfield airports.  (Para 26)
 
           The Committee is of the opinion that without a proper assessment, it will be myopic to conclude that there is no immediate need of Greenfield
 airports at Mumbai and Delhi.  The Ministry has not even estimated as to when the trigger point will occur in terms of traffic growth to justify the
 new Greenfield airports in these metro cities. It is surprising to note that even at the planning stage, the Ministry is proposing to provide a Right of
 First Refusal (ROFR) for the second airport to the airport operator at Delhi / Mumbai, thereby favouring JV route. The existing plans therefore may
 lead to a situation wherein both the existing as well as the second airports at Delhi/Mumbai will be under the management control of private
 operators.(Para 27)
 
           The Committee is also of the opinion that the Ministry should reconsider its present plan on the modernisation and restructuring of Delhi and
 Mumbai Airports keeping in view the current scenario of the domestic as well as international aviation sector.  The present plan will only create
 monopoly in Delhi and Mumbai.  The Ministry has turned a blind eye to the paradigm shift which is occurring in South East Asian and East Asian
 countries where the focus is on the development of both Greenfield and Brownfield airports together, serving the dual purpose of enhancing the
 capacity and providing healthy competition in the best interests of the aviation sector. (Para 28)
 
           The Committee notes carefully the assurance given by the Ministry that "AAI will be better off as during the period 2006-2024 the present
 value of cash flow would be Rs.1286.5 crores where as if status quo is maintained then there could be a negative present value of cash flow to AAI at
 Rs.  (-) 998.89 crore" and "post restructuring AAI will not only be able to maintain other airports in the country but also upgrade and modernize
 these airports".  However, the Committee reiterates its observations/recommendations that the Ministry should review its strategy for the
 modernisation and restructuring of Delhi and Mumbai airports.   (Para 37)

GREENFIELD AIRPORTS AT BANGALORE AND HYDERABAD
 
            The Committee is not convinced by the reply furnished by the Ministry on the Greenfield Airport at Bangalore.   It is clear from the reply that
 the clause regarding the operation of the EPC Contracts by the Joint Venture Partners did not exist in the initial International Bidding Process. The
 issue of EPC contracts was settled between the shortlisted bidders at a later stage that too at the instance of such bidders.  The Committee notes that
 the deviation from the transparent competitive bidding process can be resorted only in exceptional cases.  The Committee finds that the Ministry has
 not justified the existence of exceptional circumstances in the award of EPC contracts at BIAL to Joint Venture Partners (JVPs).  Therefore, it is
 fallacious to contend that the procedure adopted for selection of the JVP being in itself a bidding process, it is a valid ground for not adopting a
 bidding process for the realization and operation of the project.  The Committee is therefore of the opinion that the further procedures evolved in
 respect of EPC contracts do not cure the inherent lacuna in the award of such contracts to JVPs.   Moreover, the justification sought by the Ministry
 on the issue by quoting similar instances of award of EPC contracts to strategic investors in other projects by other Ministries cannot be accepted.  
 The Ministry had earlier denied the existence of the award of EPC contracts to JVPs at BIAL before the Committee and the present justification is
 merely an afterthought, if not an outright attempt to mislead the Committee.  The Committee notes that the Ministry has now issued detailed
 guidelines in this regard to all State Governments for compliance in future.   The Committee however, reiterates its recommendation that a proper
 enquiry should be conducted into the entire matter by an independent agency as to why the provision of awarding EPC by competitive mode was
 missing in the case of BIAL.   (Para 65)
 
            The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.  The Committee recommends that it should be apprised about the details of the financial
 modalities adopted in the case of Hyderabad Airport.  (Para 68)

 recommendations/observations made in the 88
th Report has recommended that the Government should reconsider the decision to close down the
 existing airport at Hyderabad on the commissioning of a new International airport.  The recommendation is reproduced below: -
“The aviation sector in the country has changed dramatically with the low cost carriers gaining ground.   The previously unviable routes are
 now proving to be profitable ones and there is stiff competition amongst the private operators to extend their reach to all parts of the country.  In this
 changed scenario, instead of reassessing its strategy, the Ministry is following the unhealthy policy of creation of monopoly by promoting only one
 airport at different metros, as in the case of Delhi and Mumbai. The Committee also notes that the justification put forward by the Ministry for the
 closure of the existing airport at Hyderabad is contrary to the rationale of the Ministry for rejecting the proposals for Greenfield airports at Delhi and
 Mumbai.  In respect of those two airports, the Ministry has maintained throughout that unless the capacity is not optimized or added in the existing
 Brownfield airport, it is not prudent to set up a Greenfield airport.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Government should reconsider the
 decision to close down the existing airport at Hyderabad on the commissioning of a new International airport.”  (Para 71)

 of the special circumstances where AAI has to maintain certain airports irrespective of commercial viability and appointment of non-official
 directors on the board.  The Committee hopes that Airports Authority of India will be given the status of 'Mini Ratna' at the earliest so that it gets
 adequate opportunity to utilize its professional excellence in the area of development and maintenance of airports in the country and recommends

            The Committee is not satisfied with the reply. In this connection, the Committee would like to invite the attention of the Ministry towards the

 reproduced below: -
“The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Ministry and feels vindicated by the developments during the fog this winter.  The
 massive disruption of flights into and out of Delhi has highlighted the gross underutilization of the costly ILS CAT-III system installed at Indira
 Gandhi International Airport.  This has resulted in the non-utilisation of the expenditure from the tax payers’ money.  It appears that the different
 airlines resort to diversion of flights instead of using the available infrastructure because it is economical for them to follow such practice rather than
 training the pilots on CAT-III system.   The Committee feels that whatever be the reasons, the passenger facilities should be paramount and they
 should not be put to any hardship.  Moreover, even if IA and AI have trained their pilots and are using the system, the diversion of flights of the
 private carriers gives adverse publicity to the civil aviation sector as a whole.  The Committee feels that there should be some penal provision to
 discourage the diversion of flights due to fog by the private operators or they should be compelled to utilise the ILS CAT-III system. The Committee
 takes note of the relevant news reports appearing in the print and visual media and the inadequate response of the Ministry thereon. The Committee
 also notes that the Ministry is now waking up to the need for the implementation of the recommendation in the face of severe public criticism. The
 Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation that in order to improve the operational efficiency during the extreme foggy conditions, training
 of pilots should be made compulsory by the private airlines on CAT-III System.  The Committee further recommends that utilization of CAT-II and
 CAT-III systems by private airlines should be made compulsory by training a fixed minimum proportion of their pilots and it should be enforced by
 the Government strictly.” (Para 105)

R E P O R T
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
 observations/recommendations contained in its Eighty-third Report on the “Functioning of the Commission of Railway
 Safety”, which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on the 6 th December, 2004 and laid on the table of Lok Sabha on 3rd
 December, 2004.
 
 2.         Action Taken Replies on some of the observations/recommendations contained in the Report were received
 from the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 26
th May, 2005 and it was informed that the complete Action Taken Replies on
